findings.description: The MSCA-PF evaluation form requires 'consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project' under the soundness of methodology sub-criterion. No gender dimension analysis is evidenced in any available artifact relating to the research methodology. The sole gender-related reference across all available inputs is ELTE's institutional obligation to maintain a gender equality plan at grant signature (implementation section 3.2) — an administrative compliance statement, not a methodological consideration. The proposal does not analyse whether gender-disaggregated patterns in irrigation decision-making, water-use behaviour, or technology adoption among the farmer user base are relevant to the research design, the demonstrator interface, or the validity of the field-validation protocol. An evaluator scoring methodology soundness under the MSCA-PF evaluation form must penalise the absence of any engagement with this sub-criterion.
findings.evidence: CC-09 terminology consistency check lists no gender-related terms among the canonical technical terms used across sections. Implementation section 3.2 states only: 'Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, as a higher education establishment in an EU Member State, is required to have a gender equality plan in place at grant signature and throughout the fellowship.'
findings.recommendation: Add a substantive analysis — even if brief — of the gender dimension's relevance (or argued irrelevance with explicit justification) to: (a) the remote-sensing and probabilistic modelling methodology itself, (b) the farmer user base and any gender-disaggregated irrigation decision or technology-adoption patterns relevant to the demonstrator's design, and (c) team composition and inclusive research practice. A one-paragraph treatment that explicitly considers and disposes of the question satisfies the sub-criterion; the current total absence does not.

findings.description: The MSCA-PF Impact sub-criterion requires 'credibility of the measures to enhance the career perspectives and employability of the researcher and contribution to his/her skills development.' The proposal deliberately and explicitly defers all specific, measurable career development targets — publication planning, training hour targets, co-supervision arrangements, and career-progression milestones — to the Career Development Plan at month 3. While procedurally compliant with SR-04, this structural choice leaves evaluators without the evidence base needed to score the career-perspectives sub-criterion at proposal stage. Evaluators cannot assess credibility of career measures that are not articulated in the proposal text.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.1 states: 'the specific, measurable training and career targets for the fellowship — publication planning, training hour targets, co-supervision, and career-progression milestones — that are intentionally not pre-asserted in this proposal; none were operator-provided at proposal stage, and the appropriate moment to fix them is at the start of the action, jointly with the supervisor.'
findings.recommendation: The Impact section should include at minimum indicative (non-binding) career development statements covering: (a) anticipated number and type of peer-reviewed outputs and approximate target journals, (b) the planned post-fellowship career trajectory (e.g., independent fellowship application, academic position, AgriTech industry role), (c) named transferable-skills training dimensions with approximate time allocations, and (d) planned networking activities (conferences, visiting seminars) that expand the fellow's professional network. These are not contractual commitments; they are the specificity evaluators require to assess credibility.

findings.description: The MSCA-PF Excellence sub-criterion 'Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills' requires evidence of research independence and competitiveness. Across all available artifacts, only one work by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is cited: the PhD thesis preprint (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527, summa cum laude, 2020). No peer-reviewed journal publications, conference contributions, independently secured grants, or other indicators of research track record beyond the doctorate appear in any available artifact. Evaluators scoring this sub-criterion expect evidence of post-doctoral or late-doctoral research output and independence.
findings.evidence: doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527 is the sole publication cited for Dr. Cholakova across the assembled draft, consistency log, and implementation section. No peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, or grants by the fellow are referenced in any available artifact.
findings.recommendation: The Excellence section should enumerate the fellow's peer-reviewed publication record (journal articles, conference proceedings), any invited talks, reviewing or editorial activities, research project contributions beyond the doctoral thesis, field-specific awards, and other evidence of research independence. If the record is limited by career stage, contextualise within career stage norms, emphasise the quality and depth of the doctoral work, and highlight any post-PhD contributions that demonstrate continued research productivity.

findings.description: The MSCA-PF Impact sub-criterion on 'the magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts' requires evidence of the project's reach and generalisability. The primary user group is Hungarian tomato growers through AgroVIR. While this pilot scope is appropriate for a 24-month single-researcher fellowship, evaluators assessing magnitude will look for evidence that the probabilistic methodology and demonstrator findings are transferable beyond the pilot crop and country. Available artifacts provide no scale evidence: no EU smallholder irrigated horticulture acreage, no addressable farmer population estimate, and no quantitative water-use efficiency improvement potential grounded in comparable interventions.
findings.evidence: CC-07 confirms impact pathways PWY-EI-01 through PWY-EI-07 map to outcomes OUT-1 through OUT-5. Implementation section 3.2 grounds the decision objective in 'Hungarian row-crop horticulture.' No quantitative scale or generalisability evidence appears in any available artifact.
findings.recommendation: The Impact section should add a scale and generalisability narrative: (a) an estimated addressable population of smallholder irrigated horticulture operations in Hungary and Central/Eastern Europe, (b) a methodological generalisation statement explaining how the probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework transfers to other crops (e.g., peppers, vine, cucumbers) and other EU geographies with equivalent satellite data coverage, and (c) an indicative water-use efficiency improvement potential drawn from analogous published studies to anchor the economic impact claim.

findings.description: The Impact sub-criterion on 'suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan' requires assessable dissemination commitments at proposal stage. The formal Dissemination and Exploitation Plan (D5-02) is deferred to month 6. In available artifacts, the dissemination strategy does not name target journals for primary research outputs, identify specific conference targets, or specify open-software and open-data repository platforms for the demonstrator code. Without these specifics, evaluators cannot confirm the suitability of dissemination channels for reaching the intended scientific and practitioner audiences.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.1 (T5-01) states the strategy 'implements the open-access publication strategy, open research software and data releases, and communication to the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing community and to Hungarian tomato growers through AgroVIR.' No journals, conferences, or repository platforms are named.
findings.recommendation: The Impact section should name: (a) 2–3 target journals appropriate for primary research outputs (e.g., Remote Sensing of Environment, Agricultural Water Management, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture), (b) at least one relevant conference target (e.g., IEEE IGARSS, EGU General Assembly, European Conference on Precision Agriculture), and (c) the planned open-software and open-data repository (e.g., GitHub + Zenodo with DOI minting). These specifics make the dissemination commitment credible and assessable without requiring additional work packages.

findings.description: RISK-04 (sparse ground-truth coverage leaving the validation statistically under-powered) is classified at medium probability and high impact. The contingency plan refers to supplementing with 'published reference datasets' without identifying any specific dataset. No sample size analysis or power calculation is provided to assure evaluators that the planned T3-01 field campaigns will generate sufficient observations to evaluate the RQ5 criterion (90% prediction-interval coverage approximately 90% of the time) with statistical confidence. For a methodology whose headline commitment is honest uncertainty quantification, the absence of a statistical design rationale for the primary validation is a credibility gap.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.1, RISK-04: 'Contingency: prioritise ground truth at a focused pilot site and supplement with published reference datasets.' The RQ5 criterion requires empirical ground-truth observations for prediction-interval coverage evaluation; no sample size rationale or power consideration is provided in the work plan or risk register.
findings.recommendation: Add a brief statistical design rationale for the T3-01 campaigns: state the approximate number of field plots, measurement visits per growing season, and expected total ground-truth observation count, and relate this to the minimum sample size needed to evaluate the 90% PI coverage criterion with reasonable confidence. Name at least one specific published reference dataset (e.g., from EC Joint Research Centre crop monitoring or published Central European agricultural field studies) that could supplement sparse campaign data if RISK-04 materialises.

findings.description: The Implementation sub-criterion on 'quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations, including hosting arrangements' extends to associated partners. AgroVIR is the sole participating organisation whose quality and capacity must be assessed alongside ELTE. The proposal describes AgroVIR only as 'the confirmed associated partner, based in Hungary' without providing any organisational profile: no founding date, operational scale, number of farm clients, geographic coverage of its farmer network, or track record in supporting research or EU-funded activities. Evaluators cannot independently verify that AgroVIR has the scale of farmer relationships required to provide statistically adequate and logistically viable field-site access for T3-01 and T3-03.
findings.evidence: Implementation section 3.2: 'AgroVIR is the confirmed associated partner, based in Hungary. AgroVIR's role is scoped and specific: farmer access, field validation logistics, and feedback at Hungarian tomato field sites.' No further organisational characterisation appears in this section or any other available artifact.
findings.recommendation: Add a 2–3 sentence organisational profile for AgroVIR in section 3.2: approximate number of farm clients or coverage of the AgroVIR farmer network, any prior involvement in research or EU-funded agricultural projects, and confirmation that a letter of commitment has been obtained or will be provided at grant signature. This allows evaluators to confirm AgroVIR's fitness for its field-access role without requiring significant additional text.

revision_actions.action_description: Insert a gender dimension and diversity sub-paragraph within the Excellence section's methodology sub-section (sub_section 1.2 or equivalent). Explicitly analyse whether gender-disaggregated patterns in irrigation decision-making, water-use behaviour, or farmer technology adoption are relevant to the research methodology, the demonstrator's interface design, or the composition and reach of the validation protocol. If the gender dimension does not substantively alter the probabilistic modelling or remote-sensing methodology, state this explicitly with a two-to-three sentence justification and note the team's commitment to gender-inclusive practices in dissemination and farmer engagement. A concise, direct engagement satisfies the sub-criterion; the current complete absence does not.

Strengthen the career development narrative in the Impact section with indicative (non-binding) targets: (a) anticipated number and type of peer-reviewed outputs (e.g., two journal articles targeting Remote Sensing of Environment and Agricultural Water Management) and approximate submission window within the 24-month fellowship, (b) an explicit post-fellowship career trajectory narrative (e.g., application for a national or ERC starting grant, academic position in geoinformatics or precision agriculture, or a role in the AgriTech industry building on the demonstrator), (c) named transferable-skills dimensions to be covered in T4-02 with indicative time allocations, and (d) any planned networking activities (named conferences, research visit to a complementary group) that broaden the fellow's professional network. These are not contractual commitments but are required for evaluators to assess career-perspectives credibility.

Expand the researcher profile sub-section in the Excellence section (sub_section 1.4 or equivalent) to enumerate: (a) all peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova with venue and year, (b) any research projects the fellow has contributed to beyond her doctoral thesis, (c) instrumentation and field measurement expertise acquired (species measured, instruments operated, measurement campaigns conducted), and (d) any awards, fellowships, or other recognition received. If the record is early-career in breadth, explicitly contextualise it within career stage and emphasise the depth and scientific quality of the doctoral contribution and any post-PhD outputs.

Add a scale and generalisability sub-paragraph to the Impact section: (a) estimate the addressable population of smallholder irrigated horticulture operations in Hungary and Central/Eastern Europe (e.g., citing Eurostat or FAO irrigated area data), (b) include a brief methodological generalisation statement explaining how the probabilistic multi-sensor fusion-to-decision framework applies to other row crops (peppers, vine, cucumbers) and other EU geographies with comparable Sentinel satellite coverage, and (c) cite at least one published study reporting water-use efficiency improvements from comparable precision irrigation interventions to provide an anchor for the economic impact claim.

Add specific dissemination channel commitments to the Impact section's dissemination sub-section: (a) name 2–3 target journals for primary research outputs (e.g., Remote Sensing of Environment, Agricultural Water Management, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture), (b) identify at least one relevant conference target (e.g., IEEE IGARSS, EGU General Assembly, European Conference on Precision Agriculture) with a rationale for audience fit, and (c) specify the open-software and open-data repository platform for the demonstrator code and datasets (e.g., GitHub repository with Zenodo archiving and DOI minting at project close). These additions make the dissemination commitment specific and assessable without changing the work plan structure.

Add a brief statistical design rationale to the Implementation section 3.1 risk assessment or work plan narrative for the T3-01 field validation campaigns: state the approximate number of field plots targeted, measurement visits planned per growing season, and resulting expected total ground-truth observation count; relate this to the minimum sample size needed to evaluate the RQ5 90% PI coverage criterion with reasonable statistical confidence. In the RISK-04 contingency, replace the generic 'published reference datasets' reference with at least one named specific dataset (e.g., the EC Joint Research Centre MARS crop monitoring dataset, or a named published Hungarian agricultural field study) that would be suitable for supplementing sparse campaign data.

Add a 2–3 sentence organisational profile for AgroVIR within Implementation section 3.2 immediately following the current introductory description: include the approximate number of farm clients or geographic coverage of the AgroVIR farmer network in Hungary, any prior involvement in agricultural research projects or EU-funded innovation activities, and a statement confirming that a letter of commitment from AgroVIR has been obtained (or will be provided at grant signature). This allows evaluators to verify AgroVIR's fitness for its field-access and farmer-feedback role without requiring substantive additional text.
